title: Met Police confirms it received 2019 letter with "number of claims" about Meghan's father
description: Markle moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes.He is reportedly now living in a Florida rehabilitation centre learning to
body: Markle moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes.He is reportedly now living in a Florida rehabilitation centre learning to walk again after having a leg amputated in 2025.Meghan's half-brother Thomas Markle Jnr claimed he found a stash of images belonging to his father at his former Philippines home, the Sun reported.He is said to have told police he discovered child abuse videos and pictures among the items. He is understood to have contacted the FBI in July.In a statement released by Meghan on Friday she said that when she received the information of the claims against her father she was "given assurance that these were being investigated".Meghan said she hoped it could be understood why she had kept her distance from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".Authorities in the Philippines have confirmed they are investigating the allegations about Meghan's father.The BBC was told on Friday the matter was being investigated by an anti-human trafficking and child sexual exploitation task force.Philippines Interior Minister Jonvic Remulla separately said national police had secured his computer and would carry out a digital forensic examination.Meghan is the only daughter of Markle and her mother Doria Ragland.He pulled out of attending Meghan and Harry's wedding in 2018 - citing ill health - and they became estranged.The duke and duchess moved to the US in 2020 after stepping down as working royals.They returned to the UK with their children this year after six years away.

schema.headline: Met Police confirms it received 2019 letter with "number of claims" about Meghan's father

title: Jazzy: The Irish DJ dropping her debut after a billion streams
description: Releasing your first album is a big step for any artist, but for Jazzy it's one that's followed some huge strides. The Irish singer and DJ has been st
body: Releasing your first album is a big step for any artist, but for Jazzy it's one that's followed some huge strides. The Irish singer and DJ has been streamed more than a billion times and worked with industry heavyweights including Calvin Harris.If that's not enough, on Saturday she has her biggest gig yet when she'll be playing tracks like No Bad Vibes and Someday in front of a home crowd in Dublin.For Jazzy, writing an album has always been in the back of her mind and now, finally, it's time to hit send.She's previously released dozens of singles, building up a monthly listenership over 10 million strong, but Peace and Patience is her first full-length work."It's been quite a few years of creating some smaller projects," she tells BBC Newsbeat."That's given me enough experience now to feel like it was the right moment."The 30-year-old, real name Yasmine Byrne, has been putting out music for more than five years and collabed with the likes of Sonny Fodera, Rossi. and KILIMANJARO on some of her biggest tracks.Dance music has boomed in recent years, with Spotify previously telling Newsbeat that since 2020 the amount under-25s listen to the genre has grown by more than 73% globally.It also dominated festival line-ups over the summer - including Radio 1's Big Weekend which dedicated all its stages to dance music on the opening night.But artists in the genre have often moved away from albums, opting instead to release EPs and singles.Jazzy has noticed the change, saying it feels "a lot different now, with people kind of siding with virality rather than quality of music"."When I was making the album, I wasn't thinking about going viral or anything like that. I just wanted to make something that was true to me and sounded like a Jazzy album."I like to let things happen quite organically and I try to just let the music speak to me."Jazzy is rooted in the Dublin club scene, starting her career as part of a group called Powerful Creative Minds in the city.But as more and more clubs close, the DJ says there are fewer opportunities for artists to cut their teeth offline. "When I first started going out, there was a lot more going on," she says. "There was a lot more nightclubs to go to and it's very different when we look at it now, which is sad."There's definitely a home for dance music on the internet of course but club culture is very important and I think that's something that we need to keep going for sure."Latest figures from the Night Time Industries Association, external suggest about 12 venues are closing across the UK every month, with almost 30% of the night time economy lost since the coronavirus pandemic. "I hope to God that it doesn't disappear, the club scene altogether," says Jazzy, who describes a similar issue in Ireland."We all need to try and put a hand in to keep it going."Jazzy's taking her new album on tour across the UK from next month, but first she has her biggest gig yet: Dublin's 3Arena in front of a home crowd.Even after a Coachella set and supporting Calvin Harris, she describes this as the "biggest milestone of my career to date".While she says fans can mostly expect her brand of uplifting records on the album, she says it's also more personal than her usual work.She highlights one track in particular, Invisible, as a change from her more upbeat releases. It deals with a bad experience she had in the music industry, describing it as "like my first ever diss track"."I hope [fans] learn a little bit more about me, because that was one of my goals with the album - to open up a little bit about experiences in life as well. "So there's a little message from me in each song."

schema.headline: Jazzy: The Irish DJ dropping her debut after a billion streams

title: UK braces for worst of Storm Boelo as amber warnings due to come into force
description: Amber weather warnings are due to come into force in northern parts of the UK as the worst weather from Storm Boelo approaches.Strong winds and heavy
body: Amber weather warnings are due to come into force in northern parts of the UK as the worst weather from Storm Boelo approaches.Strong winds and heavy showers are expected to intensify through Saturday evening, with widespread gusts of 60 to 70mph expected to hit Scotland.Amber wind warnings from the Met Office will come into force from 21:00 BST for parts of Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England, bringing an increased risk of travel disruption and potential risk to life.The second named storm in as many days comes as National Grid continues to restore power to thousands of properties in south-west England after the area was hit hardest by Storm Austen.The National Grid said on Saturday that more than 124,000 properties had been restored with power supplies since the beginning of the storm. However, hundreds were still without power on Saturday evening.Storm Boelo is set to cause disruption throughout the rest of the weekend, with the amber warning in Scotland due to stay in place for 24 hours.Forecasters have warned of strong winds with gusts to 80mph expected in exposed coastal areas.These winds could cause power cuts, flying debris, damage to buildings and trees, travel disruption and danger to life from large waves, the Met Office said.The strongest winds will affect western Scotland first on Saturday evening, before spreading eastwards overnight and through Sunday.The Met Office has warned that being outside in high winds could make people "more vulnerable to injury", stating: "Stay indoors as much as possible. If you do go out, try not to walk, or shelter, close to buildings and trees."Parts of Northern Ireland have also been issued with an amber warning, from 21:00 on Saturday to 10:00 on Sunday.Meanwhile, yellow rain warnings have been issued for the south-west, north-west and south-east of England, the West Midlands and Wales until 23:00 on Saturday.Much of the north of England and Scotland has a yellow wind warning in place, which is set to last until 21:00 on Sunday, and Northern Ireland's yellow wind warning will be in place until midday on Sunday.Jason Kelly, the Met Office's chief forecaster, said: "People should prepare for the potential for disruption, particularly to travel and power supplies. Secure loose items outside, plan ahead if you are travelling and keep up to date with the latest forecast and warnings for your area."

schema.headline: UK braces for worst of Storm Boelo as amber warnings due to come into force

title: Nicky Hayen: Burnley head coach sacked after just 14 games
description: Head coach Nicky Hayen has been sacked after just 14 games in charge at Burnley following a poor start to the season.Hayen's final match was Saturday'
body: Head coach Nicky Hayen has been sacked after just 14 games in charge at Burnley following a poor start to the season.Hayen's final match was Saturday's 4-1 defeat at Lincoln City, as the hosts came back from 1-0 down to emphatically condemn the Clarets to a sixth defeat of the campaign and leave them 22nd in the Championship.Belgian Hayen was only appointed on 10 July to succeed Scott Parker, who left at the end of April days after the Clarets' relegation from the Premier League was confirmed.Burnley announced the news with a short two-sentence statement within two hours of their defeat at the ProAmpac Stadium.Speaking in his post-match press conference, Hayen had said: "I'm not going to lose my energy because this is something out of my hands" with reference to his future.Hayen won the Belgian title with Club Brugge in 2024 and was brought in by owner Alan Pace to oversee a promotion bid, with the Clarets having gone up in their last two Championship campaigns in 2023 and 2025.But after a promising draw with West Ham on the opening weekend, their season has nosedived and the club are without a win at home in the league since beating Leeds United at Turf Moor in the Premier League over a year ago.The Clarets earned a first win of the season in style earlier this month as they returned from the extended international break to beat struggling Watford 4-0 but then drew against Charlton and lost to Wolves, scoring first in both matches.Saturday's defeat to the Imps also means they have won just one of the past 24 league games and have conceded 25 goals from their opening 12 Championship games - the worst record in the division.

schema.headline: Nicky Hayen: Burnley head coach sacked after just 14 games

title: Ukraine says Starlink connection 'now stable' after network limits
description: Ukraine now has a "stable connection" to Starlink, its defence minister has said, after its military suffered days of restricted connectivity on the s
body: Ukraine now has a "stable connection" to Starlink, its defence minister has said, after its military suffered days of restricted connectivity on the satellite internet network.Kyiv relies on the Starlink and its military-grade counterpart Starshield for piloting drones and operations within Ukraine, but last week accused US President Donald Trump of telling owner Elon Musk to place limits on it. This meant drones would lose connection when travelling at 161km/h (100mph) or more, it said. Trump denied doing so before saying Musk had "put it back".Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said that speeds of more than 400km/h were now possible on the network, indicating that full capability had been restored."This result is above all important for our front, for our soldiers, for the operation of drones, for logistics and for communications," he said in a statement on Saturday.Ukraine's military uses the network of 10,000 low Earth orbit satellites extensively for military operations, particularly in remote areas on the battlefield. Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, which Musk said was controlled by the US military when he suggested the Pentagon could be behind the recent issues.Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles or drones deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.The debacle over Starlink began last week, and emerged during a broader diplomatic row between Trump and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.Faced with midterm elections next month, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the US market - a move criticised by Ukraine and its European allies.Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, have pushed global prices higher.While the attacks have had an impact on global fuel prices, rises seen this year have primarily been due to the Iran war.Zelensky said that, as well as seemingly limiting Starlink capability in Ukraine, the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump also denied.Meanwhile, fighting on the ground continues.Russia's ministry of defence wrote on Telegram on Saturday that their air defences shot down 616 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones, striking a number of regions across the country, including Russian-annexed Crimea.Sergey Aksyonov, the region's Moscow-backed governor, said restrictions on electricity and water had been put in place because of power cuts caused by the drone strike.Meanwhile, Ukrainian authorities said they struck a missile component manufacturer, a chemical plant and an aircraft at a military airfield inside Russia in the past 24 hours.They also said that Russia carried out 88 air strikes using 309 glide bombs and 10,270 kamikaze drones on Friday.

schema.headline: Ukraine says Starlink connection 'now stable' after network limits

title: Don't fall for this - how to protect yourself from AI scams
description: Be careful where you buy from, shoppers are being warned as criminals use AI to supercharge scams.Some fraudsters have made websites for fake retailer
body: Be careful where you buy from, shoppers are being warned as criminals use AI to supercharge scams.Some fraudsters have made websites for fake retailers that claim to be family-owned firms selling quality UK-made products. Images may show a UK High Street with Union Jack flags in shot.If you order you're likely to find a product either never arrives, or is a cheap, mass-produced item from a country such as China, trading standards officers say. AI-generated images like this, as well as voice cloning and deepfake videos are increasingly being used to trick people out of their money, according to National Trading Standards.For the first time, it has drawn up an AI scam watchlist, external highlighting some of the tools and techniques criminals are using.

schema.headline: Don't fall for this - how to protect yourself from AI scams

title: Moment giant fin whale caught feeding off Pembrokeshire coast
description: To avoid causing harm to the whales while recording out at sea, Morgan said: "We do what we can to keep our distance in the boat but unfortunately nat
body: To avoid causing harm to the whales while recording out at sea, Morgan said: "We do what we can to keep our distance in the boat but unfortunately nature can have a mind of its own sometimes."There's been times when we've been anchored up fishing with nothing happening in the area and a whale has popped up next to us."The wildlife will approach you sometimes."Dr Marianna Chimienti is a lecturer in marine top predator ecology at Bangor University and said Morgan experienced a "rare and fortunate encounter".Chimienti, who specialises in animal behaviour added: "It is normal that the fin whale comes and feeds at the surface, as it is part of the species foraging strategy but being in the coastal water is quite spectacular."In theory, they should have migrated."Little is known about fin whale migration but their movements are believed to be quite different from other baleen whales such as blues and humpbacks. Scientists have found that fin whales are more abundant in higher latitudes in warmer months of the year, and more numerous in lower latitudes during colder months, but this can vary.

schema.headline: Moment giant fin whale caught feeding off Pembrokeshire coast

title: Women's Super League: Arsenal release pressure but can they kick on?
description: Arsenal started the day in the bottom half of the table, four points off fourth-placed Tottenham and 12 points behind leaders Manchester City.With the
body: Arsenal started the day in the bottom half of the table, four points off fourth-placed Tottenham and 12 points behind leaders Manchester City.With their title ambitions in ruins, manager Renee Slegers was facing weekly questions about her future and defeat by Spurs could have been the last straw.Confidence was at an all-time low and a high-stakes north London derby was not the ideal game to go into with no momentum.The nerves were obvious as there were misplaced passes, poor clearances and sloppy errors in a disjointed first half. Tottenham had even taken the lead, although they held it for just four minutes as Georgia Stanway's powerful strike cancelled out a header from Cathinka Tandberg.When asked what she said to the players at half-time, boss Slegers revealed: "I just gave constructive and tactical things that could help us to get the win, and remind us about the fight and intensity on the pitch. "It was a real derby. The team were in a good place and were finding solutions themselves. It was just constructive messaging."Arsenal were much better in the second half, putting more pressure on Tottenham and getting the winning goal they needed.Referee Phoebe Cross pointed to the spot when Lisa Baum's shot bounced off the post and Tandberg's clearance hit the outstretched hand of her Spurs team-mate Ella Morris nearby.Alessia Russo, who had failed to convert a big chance just moments earlier, made no mistake the second time around and slotted the ball past goalkeeper Lize Kop.She roared in celebration and sprinted towards the away fans - an outburst of emotion that was replicated at full-time by England team-mate Leah Williamson.Slegers stood back as her players enjoyed the adulation from supporters. They had finally delivered a win and the fans had something to sing about."I'm so happy we got it for them. We said we would play for the fans. We played for them and connected with them," said Slegers. "We sold out the away section, they came in the rain and sang and fought with us throughout the game. "At the end, it was scrappy and it was game management and they were all there with us."You could see how the team responded and how they were with the fans. It was pure joy and happiness. We want to capitalise on these emotions."It was the perfect result, but never easy.Former Arsenal defender Gilly Flaherty told BBC One the visitors were "causing their own problems" in an unconvincing first half and they took time to settle.They showed nervousness and had to cling on at the end, relying on a stroke of luck and a controversial refereeing decision to get them over the line.But it was not undeserved and Slegers made the decision at full-time to show their feelings and celebrate with supporters in a different way, having abandoned their familiar post-match team huddle in the centre of the pitch."The fans were on our minds. We wanted to play for something bigger, not only for ourselves. That is always a balance," she said.One Gunners fan told BBC Sport at half-time: "It's 1-1 but Arsenal look very nervy in and out of possession. Another week, another formation, another different starting XI. All feels so desperate and out of control."Slegers showed understanding of their frustration as she added: "We normally do a huddle on the pitch but we decided to just go to the fans instead. "Actions speak louder than words. There was not much more talking to do so we just wanted to celebrate with them."We had a run of games where results haven't been good enough. It was frustrating for everyone. This will definitely energise us."Slegers is pleased Arsenal are set to embark on a busy period with their next game in the Women's Champions League on Wednesday against Benfica.They have four home games in November and a trip to Barcelona - all good opportunities to build momentum.Their WSL title hopes may be gone, but a top-three finish is imperative to secure European football next season."We need to back this up in the next couple of games. There were some really good things for us on the pitch," said Slegers."We want to be more consistent but this was a really good step. It's positive energy we want to capitalise on, but it's only a step."

schema.headline: Women's Super League: Arsenal release pressure but can they kick on?

title: Sam Fender calls out ticket prices ahead of 2027 tour sale
description: Sam Fender has called out the price of gig tickets ahead of his next tour, promising to lower the cost.The 32-year-old announced his Proper Massive St
body: Sam Fender has called out the price of gig tickets ahead of his next tour, promising to lower the cost.The 32-year-old announced his Proper Massive Stadium Tour earlier this week, which will visit Newcastle, Cardiff, London, Edinburgh, Dublin and Manchester in summer 2027.While tickets are yet to go on sale, Fender responded to a post on social media which claimed to outline the expected ticket prices.The Geordie musician also said standing would not be split into a front and back tier and he had "no idea how this was normalised at gigs".Tickets are due to go on general sale at 09:30 GMT on Friday, with a pre-sale at the same time on Wednesday.But Fender said he was "not happy" with the reported prices."They're getting changed," he said on Instagram."It got inflated well more than I'd had in mind, it should only be inflated in relation to the cost of putting the show on."The North Shields singer also said he did not want there to be an option for fans to pay more money to be closer to the front."The standing will not be split as well, I had no idea about it," Fender said."I have no idea how this was normalised in gigs... it won't be happening on this tour."He is not the first musician to raise concerns over ticket pricing.Zara Larsson agreed with fans earlier this year that her tickets were too expensive.The Swedish singer said while she did not have control over the prices, she hoped she would in the future. Follow BBC North East on X, external, Facebook, external, Nextdoor and Instagram, external and listen to Radio Newcastle on BBC Sounds.

schema.headline: Sam Fender calls out ticket prices ahead of 2027 tour sale

title: UK state pension: How does it compare with other countries?
description: Image source, 10000 hours Getty ImagesByDharshini DavidDeputy economics editorGetting older is something few of us want to think about. Yet how we fun
body: Image source, 10000 hours Getty ImagesByDharshini DavidDeputy economics editorGetting older is something few of us want to think about. Yet how we fund our later years, and how much we'll get, has been a hot topic.The triple lock formula - state pensions increasing by the greatest of 2.5%, earnings growth, or inflation - means those benefits have risen far faster than the earnings of workers since its introduction in 2011.But as housing costs have also been rising fast, pensioner poverty has actually increased slightly in the last decade.Nevertheless, even if you take those costs into consideration, pensioners are less likely to be in relative poverty - that is, having to get by on less than 60% of the income of the typical household - than families with children or working-age people.And funding the triple lock has already cost the state billions more than initially envisaged. With that cost set to balloon further, the debate over whether that is sustainable, or fair, has raged for a while.Andy Burnham intends to start a new system in a few years, which would see the state pension increase by at least inflation or 2.5%, and remove the automatic annual link with average earnings. It will likely mean less generous increases, although it will keep track with earnings growth over the longer term.But are pensioners being short-changed in other ways? How do we compare with other countries? One way of measuring that is to look at how generous the typical pension is relative to workers' average earnings - the replacement rate. The OECD considers the outlook for those born at the start of the millennium in different countries on average wages, and assumes the pension system as it existed in 2022 is in place.On that basis, looking at the basic state pension, retirement benefits in the UK look low compared with other wealthy countries. And that is even when you consider that our system compels workers to be automatically enrolled in occupational schemes. If you consider both of those, then after tax, UK retirement benefits would be 54.2% of average UK earnings, compared with an average of 63.2% across wealthy countries.But then there is income from other occupational and personal pensions, which are more prevalent in the UK. Include those and the gap narrows. However, that does also mean that those relying on just the state pension for their incomes are a fair bit worse off than many retired people elsewhere.So does that make the case for boosting spending on public pensions in the UK? Well, the amount spent on the state pension is set to top £150bn a year, the single most expensive benefit to fund. But other figures from the OECD show that the UK state spends a lower amount on total retirement benefits, relative to the size of its economy, than the average wealthy country.But there are two issues to consider. Firstly, this is about political choices, and the UK chooses to dedicate larger amounts to items such as universal healthcare.And secondly, with ageing populations, the OECD reckons the amount needed for pensions may be set to soar in many nations by 2060 (the exceptions largely being those that are deploying changes). Its predictions for the UK are likely to rise by less under the revised triple lock system being put in place by Andy Burnham but it may still mean more borrowing. As it is, £1 in every £13 the UK government spends is to pay the interest on existing debt. And countries with more generous pensions, such as Italy, have faced pressure to reform.So in many ways, with auto-enrolment into workplace pensions, the UK appears to be ahead of the game in insisting on universal privately funded pensions for workers. But that system raises another issue: the gender pension gap. The gender pension gap is the difference between the average pension income of men and women aged 65 and over, as a percentage of men's average pension income.It found that the typical gap in most wealthy countries is around 22.8% in favour of men. But in the UK women typically get a pension that is a third less than what a man gets - in the main, due to the reliance on private pensions - although it should be noted that the most recent data the OECD has for the UK is for 2021.Women are more likely to have received lower pay over the course of their working lives, taken career breaks or worked part time. And the hit to pension pots can be stark.So step back and look at the big picture and British pensioners - and those who have yet to retire - may feel others have it better elsewhere. But the message from all of this isn't to dwell on outrage but to take action. The state pension has become more generous over the years, but if you want to enjoy the same kind of retirement as those elsewhere, get saving.That is - if you can, and if you haven't left it too late.Get in touchDo you have any views, comments or questions about this story?

schema.headline: UK state pension: How does it compare with other countries?

title: Aston Villa 2-1 Man City: Gianluigi Donnarumma and Marc Guehi under spotlight
description: Manchester City's 100% winning start to the Premier League season came to an abrupt end against Aston Villa - leaving Enzo Maresca with glaring defens
body: Manchester City's 100% winning start to the Premier League season came to an abrupt end against Aston Villa - leaving Enzo Maresca with glaring defensive issues to resolve.Nicolas Jackson's double in a 2-1 home win for Villa means City have now managed only one clean sheet in their past six games and the form of goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma and defender Marc Guehi is of concern.Since the start of last season, only eight players have made more errors leading to Premier League goals than Donnarumma and Guehi with three each.City's most recent shutout came in their impressive victory at Liverpool two weeks ago but, around that game, City have conceded against teams ranging from Champions League holders Paris St-Germain to top-flight strugglers Sunderland.Maresca was forced to try different combinations at the back against Villa, but as the legendary Sir Alex Ferguson once said, "attack wins you games, defence wins you titles".Though still early days in the campaign and guaranteed to be in the top two come the end of the weekend, City need to shore up their backline if they are to stay there.By contrast, title rivals Arsenal moved level on points at the top of the table later in the day with a comfortable 2-0 win at home to Everton.The Gunners have conceded just five goals in eight matches, with Saturday's goals coming from centre-backs Ezri Konsa and Gabriel.That's back-to-back Premier League clean sheets for Mikel Arteta's men, with the luxury of centre-back William Saliba still to come back into the side.Only Manchester United - 1.16 in 1996-97 and 1.18 in 1999-00 - have won the Premier League title with a goals against rate worse than Man City's current 1.13 per game. Arsenal's goals against rate is currently 0.625 per game.Asked if the two goals the conceded were avoidable, Maresca told TNT Sports: "Absolutely, both. "Sometimes you have to be a bit more lucky because we only conceded those two chances, but we created a lot of chances."We played most of the game in their box but you have to be clinical and avoid mistakes like the two goals we conceded."City were undone by goals in each half from the brilliant Jackson at a raucous Villa Park to end their streak of seven straight wins at the start of this campaign.Maresca's team started the season by conceding eight goals in their first nine games but that has seen a dramatic downturn, with nine goals hitting the back of their net in the past four matches.The signing of Donnarumma last summer was heralded as the acquisition of one of the best goalkeepers in the world to replace Ederson.The Brazilian changed the face of English football with his footwork, spraying short and long passes across the pitch, and there are few keepers who can come close to matching that.But Italy captain Donnarumma struggles with the ball at his feet and often puts his team-mates in trouble with passes out from the back.On Saturday, City captain Ruben Dias gesticulated to his team-mate to send the ball up the pitch after the Portuguese failed to control a difficult pass.Maresca decided to sell James Trafford to Leeds for £45m in the summer, and the England international has been impressive at Elland Road.Trafford has made more passes than Donnarumma this season, has a slightly better rate at preventing goals and has come out to sweep the ball 11 times compared with Donnarumma's one.Though Donnarumma could do little about Jackson's thumping finish for the opening goal, he should have done better for the second as a low shot seemed to squirm under him.Former City defender Steph Houghton said on BBC Radio 5 Live: "I think Villa really utilised keeping the ball and being a real threat to Manchester City. Donnarumma, especially with the second goal, could probably have done a little bit better."But I don't want to take anything away from Villa. I think they performed really, really well and the gameplan was spot on, just to nullify City as much as possible."Centre-back Guehi's £20m arrival from Crystal Palace in January was considered a bargain.But it was his loose pass at Everton late last season which cost City dearly in the title race, drawing that game and losing the impetus to eventual champions Arsenal.This season has been a struggle for the England defender, culpable for both goals scored by Ipswich last weekend and being picked off by John McGinn deep in his own half for Villa's first goal.Later in the half, he hauled down Jackson on the edge of the box before being shown a yellow card, and was put out of his misery by being taken off at half-time.City sources had said they were targeting signing a right-back in the summer before pivoting elsewhere, saying Abdukodir Khusanov can provide back-up should Matheus Nunes not be available.Khusanov started out wide but struggled before being moved inside in place of Guehi, while Rico Lewis was brought to fill the gap, with Maresca acknowledging afterwards he needs to "find that balance" in defence.Villa supporters provided constant reminders to the travelling fans of their side being "cheats", and the vitriol faced following the guilty verdict of the financial charges may be beginning to weigh on the players' minds.Asked by BBC Sport if Guehi's form is a worry, Maresca said: "No, I'm not worried about Marc at all."I know he is playing every minute since the season started with us and the national team, so it's not easy but the change was also because he was on a yellow card."The way we want to be aggressive sometimes, to have one yellow card can be dangerous but I am not worried at all."Maresca, though, should be concerned by coming up against Fabian Hurzeler's free-scoring Brighton twice next week - in the Carabao Cup on Wednesday, and Premier League on Saturday.The Italian needs to fix the defensive leaks before they become something more serious.

schema.headline: Aston Villa 2-1 Man City: Gianluigi Donnarumma and Marc Guehi under spotlight

title: Strictly Come Dancing's new hosts: Flat-footed or fab-u-lous?
description: Strictly's new presenters - after frosty reviews have they warmed up?Image caption, Josh Widdicombe, Emma Willis and Johannes Radebe have adapted Tess
body: Strictly's new presenters - after frosty reviews have they warmed up?Image caption, Josh Widdicombe, Emma Willis and Johannes Radebe have adapted Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman's "keep dancing" move for threeByIan YoungsCulture reporterStrictly Come Dancing's new hosting trio received a very mixed reception when the latest series began a month ago. Ratings have dipped and the jury's still out, but critics say they are slowly getting into the groove.Changing the hosting team on the BBC's flagship Saturday night entertainment show was never likely to be a waltz in the park.And going from two presenters to three, and giving them slightly different roles, upset the show's rhythm even more.Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman were always going to be a hard act to follow.Into their sparkly shoes have stepped the safe and smooth Emma Willis; the flamboyant former professional dancer Johannes Radebe; and cheeky comedian Josh Widdicombe, a wildcard who was not hitherto associated with either the dance world or prime-time TV.Willis and Widdicombe have been paired on the live shows, where he is tasked with injecting humour into the moments before and after each dance - with mixed results, say critics.Radebe, meanwhile, has taken over from Winkleman upstairs on the mezzanine, bringing his warmth and dance expertise to the celebrity interviews following each routine.Image caption, The new hosts joined the judges on the dance floor when the series beganAfter they made their debuts in September, the Times' Carol Midgley billed them as, external "TV's most awkward ménage à trois".The Daily Telegraph's Chris Bennion declared, external that Strictly's "new 'throuple' is an utter disaster", adding: "It's a mess, a muddle, a confusing pudding."Metro's Adam Miller said, external their debut was "a triumph", however, and the i Paper's Sarah Carson wrote, external that Strictly had "played a blinder", even though the hosts "looked a little awkward as a three at times".Widdicombe has come in for particular flack. He "felt like an awkward spare part" and looked like "the work experience boy", wrote Sasha Morris of the Daily Express, external.And the Independent's Isobel Lewis said, external Widdicombe "is a problem the show needs to solve".She believes things have now improved, although the show hasn't completely solved the problem."He's basically acting too much like a comedian to be a presenter," the freelance culture journalist tells BBC News."I think he's getting more comfortable with it. When it's him and Emma doing the bits when they intro each act, and they're obviously reading off an autocue, they feel way more confident there, and it feels more like it works."Image caption, Widdicombe has been at the centre of comic sketches with the other hosts and judgesThe problem grows when Widdicombe does what comes naturally as a good comedian, Lewis says, and tries to be spontaneous."They've got, like, 20 seconds with each judge. It's such a tight amount of time, and that's what lends it to feeling sloppy and like he's constantly jumping in."Unfortunately it reads a bit like trying to steal attention and have the last laugh. I actually don't think that is what he's trying to do as a selfish act. I just think that is his comedic impulse."She says it's unfair to put the criticism on Widdicombe, and says as time has gone on he feels less awkward, with comments online suggesting some fans are "warming to him"."But at the beginning there's always that knee-jerk reaction of, 'I don't like this'," Lewis says.Image caption, Emma Willis has hosted shows including Big Brother and The VoiceRadio Times TV and podcast editor Caroline Frost agrees that the trio have gradually settled in."I think it's fair to say there were some bumps in the road in the first couple of episodes," she says, "but they do appear to be very slowly relaxing into their new roles."When it comes to Willis and Widdicombe's double act, Frost would like to see more spontaneity, not less."They've been relying quite visibly on scripts and gags, and I would like to see them relax into themselves," she adds."It's completely understandable that they would be very scripted, very alert to the clock and to all of the other many demands of running a live show of that scale - but the really talented people can do that on the fly."Josh is very likeable, and we know he's a very funny man," she notes. "He doesn't need the shackles of the script that he's currently handcuffed to, and I would love to see him take off those cuffs and become more spontaneous."Image caption, One episode featured Widdicombe and Willis in a Mary Poppins-inspired sketchFrost suggests sending Widdicombe upstairs to conduct the post-dance interviews instead of Radebe, who at times struggles to control his exuberant former fellow dancers. "It's a bit like when you get an internal promotion at work," she reflects.The producers should make the most of Radebe's strengths and make him "a sort of talent pundit", she suggests."Have him in the rehearsal rooms, telling us what's going on. He would be a lovely middleman between what we're seeing on the dance floor and what is going on technically."Ahead of the series, there had been reports that Radebe would be used as a "roving reporter".Widdicombe previously suggested the trio's roles would be fluid, telling The Rest Is Entertainment it was "going to be like total football... We're going to be moving everywhere".Image source, Guy Levy / Ray Burmiston / BBCImage caption, Radebe has already gained a reputation for his flamboyant fashionBut while some segments are flexible - especially in the Sunday result show - their main roles appear fixed.Some fans have been won over by Radebe since he took over Winkleman's old domain."JoJo has been really brilliant up in... I guess the Claudatorium, but I'm not sure what we call it now," says Flo Sayers, co-host of the Strictly on the Sofa podcast."He is the link to previous Strictly, and I think he has taken to that role really well. I like that he's a bit different from Claudia. He's less the comedian and more the supportive friend for the contestants when they've got off the dance floor and they're probably feeling a little bit vulnerable."And his fashion has been amazing, so I'm excited to see what he wears every week."Sayers isn't sure whether the new line-up has contributed to lower ratings - about six million people are tuning in every week this year, down by about a million.But overall, she believes that the trio are getting used to the demands of the series.Image caption, The presenting trio watched on as Dame Sarah Storey and dance partner Julian Caillon were eliminated last weekendDr Karen Wood, associate professor at the Centre for Dance Research at Coventry University, agrees and says the trio "are now really starting to feel a bit more settled"."I think JoJo has transitioned beautifully from professional dancer to host, and obviously he comes with all his fabulousness," she says."He's able to talk about the technical details as well as be very supportive to the professional dancers and the celebrities. And his outfits are just marvellous. So I think he suits that role very well."Likewise, Emma is holding her own when she's with Josh and when she's not. She's an experienced presenter. You can you can tell."And Josh is bringing the humour. I know it's come with some criticism. But last week was the first week that I felt, oh, these two are actually funny."She concludes: "It's really feeling like they're finding their stride and their rhythm with it. And I think that's going to develop more and more - very much as the celebrities do."Just as the show's celebrity contestants improve week by week, the same may be true of the hosts - except viewers can't vote them off if they don't like them.The next episode of Strictly Come Dancing airs on BBC One at 18:30 BST on Saturday.

schema.headline: Strictly Come Dancing's new hosts: Flat-footed or fab-u-lous?

title: Nicolas Jackson: Striker caps fine start to Aston Villa career with two goals to beat Manchester City
description: Saturday's win was achieved on the fourth anniversary of Emery's appointment as Villa boss.Under the Spaniard, they have become fixtures in the upper
body: Saturday's win was achieved on the fourth anniversary of Emery's appointment as Villa boss.Under the Spaniard, they have become fixtures in the upper echelons of the Premier League, regulars in European competition and ended a 30-year wait for a major trophy by winning the Europa League.Results are one thing, but there are also numerous examples of players who have been rejuvenated or scaled new heights in their careers under Emery's management at Villa Park.Former Scotland defender Rachel Corsie, who had a spell playing in the Women's Super League for Aston Villa late in her career, told BBC Radio 5 Live: "Emery is quite unique. A lot of coaches will focus on the tactical detail, but he's so intense with it."I remember from when I was here that his car is always at the training ground. I know people will say that's a natural thing and the life of a manager, but I would say it's an incredible amount of time."He loves to get the detail right. He never gets tired of trying to better people individually and that takes an incredible amount of work. So many players come here, improve and thrive."Jackson has prior experience of playing under Emery, having been coached by him at Villarreal, where he spent three years before Chelsea signed him for £35m.Emery told BBC Match of the Day: "I knew him at Villarreal and he started playing the level he is now. I know his capacity to exploit his qualities and I know, as well, his humility."The mentality is coming through - how focused he is in life and professional career."Speaking to TNT Sports, Jackson added: "It's not easy [to settle at a new club] but easier because of the coach and the players."It's an incredible dressing room with an incredible manager. I'm very happy to be here and hopefully I will score many goals."

schema.headline: Nicolas Jackson: Striker caps fine start to Aston Villa career with two goals to beat Manchester City

title: My dream of being a paramedic helped me save a life at 15
description: When aspiring paramedic Ethan ordered three resuscitation manikins so he could teach CPR to others, he had no idea how quickly he would put his traini
body: When aspiring paramedic Ethan ordered three resuscitation manikins so he could teach CPR to others, he had no idea how quickly he would put his training into practice and help save a life.Just two weeks after the dummies arrived at his home in Mansfield Woodhouse, in Nottinghamshire, the 15-year-old found himself performing CPR on a man he found collapsed in the street.Ethan, who had completed a one-off CPR course with East Midlands Ambulance Service (EMAS) last year, said he went through "a million and one emotions" as he realised he was about to apply his knowledge to a real-life emergency."It was adrenaline like never before, but I knew I had to stay calm, and not think too hard about the immense pressure of putting someone's life in your hands," he added.The teenager was on his way home from a casual gardening job at about 14:30 BST on 18 September when he saw a 75-year-old man slumped over "half in the road and half on the pavement" on Ley Lane.Ethan described the man as being unresponsive with a "raspy-sort of breathing" known as agonal breathing, and he was in cardiac arrest.Having completed his course with EMAS, and watching countless TV programmes about front-line emergency workers, Ethan's training kicked in.Ethan, a Year 10 pupil at The Manor Academy, said a lady who was on the phone to 999 was happy for him to take control as she did not know how to do chest compressions.Together, they moved the man to a safe, flat surface, where Ethan knew the CPR would be more effective.He said: "Even though I've spent ages preparing for this moment, to put it into practice was completely different."Ethan was soon joined at the scene by an off-duty carer from King's Mill Hospital and a teacher from a nearby primary school, who took turns with the compressions.He said it was a "massive sense of relief" when the paramedics arrived and prepared a defibrillator, and he felt a sense of hope once he saw the man had a "shockable rhythm". According to Resuscitation Council UK (RCUK), an expert organisation on resuscitation, survival rates for cardiac arrests outside hospital "remain low", with one in 13 people surviving in the East Midlands.The organisation said the statistic highlighted a need to improve confidence in CPR and using defibrillators in the region.Ethan told the BBC he was thrilled to hear from the man's family that he was making a steady recovery.The man who Ethan helped wishes to remain anonymous while he continues his recovery but his daughter, Erica, said: "As a family, we are so grateful for the bravery that Ethan showed and our gratitude for assisting saving his life. "If it wasn't for Ethan and other passing public, there would have been a very different outcome."It is incredibly important that people know at least the basics of life saving and we support Ethan totally on his journey [to becoming a paramedic] and will help where we can."Ethan became interested in learning basic life-saving skills from the age of 11 while helping to care for his grandparents.He bought the £60 resuscitation manikins with the aim of running free life-saving sessions, particularly for young people, and has already led training at local scout groups. He believes young people are reluctant to learn CPR because they feel awkward about "putting their hands on someone else".He said: "There needs to be awareness that people performing CPR are protected by the Sarah Act."The Sarah Act is also known as the the Social Action, Responsibility and Heroism Act 2015, which is designed to protect people who help others or intervene in emergencies.Robert Gladwin, head teacher of The Manor Academy, said he would now look at investing some money to help more pupils learn life-saving skills.He added: "Quite often young people get a bad reputation but, actually, this shows we generate students who have a real community value."It is absolutely critical that a Year 10 boy took charge of a situation that most people wouldn't know what to do with, and actually made a difference to the family and the wider community."Jay Astles, clinical improvement manager for out of hospital cardiac arrest at EMAS, praised "Ethan for stepping forward to help in what must have been a very stressful situation".He added: "We would encourage people of all ages to learn CPR and how to use a defibrillator. "As Ethan's experience shows, having the confidence to act in an emergency could help save a life."

schema.headline: My dream of being a paramedic helped me save a life at 15

title: How to heat your home without turning on the heating
description: Before you crank up the thermostat, try these tips to keep you and your home warmer for longerImage source, Cora HarrisonImage caption, Cora Harrison
body: Before you crank up the thermostat, try these tips to keep you and your home warmer for longerImage source, Cora HarrisonImage caption, Cora Harrison says she saves money by only turning on heating in rooms her family is usingByGrace DeanAs the UK braces for a chilly weekend, with powerful winds and heavy rain hitting parts of the country, people are looking for ways to bring some warmth to their homes without cranking up the heating just yet. It is autumn after all.But with rising energy prices making heating homes more expensive, taking action now could pay off in the long run.Experts warn, though, that if you're elderly or vulnerable you shouldn't compromise your health.To help you prepare for the chillier months, BBC News asked families and experts to share their tips for keeping your home warm and cost-effective.Eat hearty winter meals to warm you throughWhen it gets cold, many people turn to hot water bottles and blankets - but there are other ways to warm your body.The British Heart Foundation recommends wearing lots of thin layers, rather than one thick layer, to trap the heat in.Natalie, 29, says she's replaced some of the clothes she wears round the house with supermarket thermal leggings and tops and says "it's made such a difference".Amber Waring, 27, from Devon, says she eats warm meals like stews and pasta bakes, and dances round the kitchen with her toddler while they cook to help keep warm. Image source, Amber WaringImage caption, Amber Waring turns to warming meals such as pasta bake, fish pie and stew  Place a blanket under the bedsheetWith the clocks going back this weekend, the nights will be drawing in. So if you have a thicker duvet, now is the time to bring it out. Some supermarkets sell winter duvets for under £20 - look for 10.5 tog or higher.But there's something to be said for a craftily placed blanket, too. When it gets cold, Rebecca, 44, from Hertfordshire, sleeps with a blanket underneath her mattress, which she says stops draughts. "This was passed to me by my nan, she swore by it," she says. Others swear by placing a blanket above the mattress but under the bedsheet.You can heat your bed before getting in with a hot water bottle, but make sure you check the expiry date. A guide by NHS Scotland, external says to let the water from the kettle cool for a few minutes before filling, only fill it two-thirds full, squeeze air out of the top before putting the stopper on, and don't hold it directly against your skin.Using an electric blanket - to heat your bed before you get in or to wrap around yourself on the sofa - is "one of the cheapest ways" to stay warm, says Emily Seymour, energy editor at consumer organisation Which?. Testing by Which?, external shows it typically costs between 2p and 8p an hour to run an electric blanket at its highest setting. The London Fire Brigade, external says to unplug your blanket before you get into bed unless it has a thermostat control, not to use a hot water bottle at the same time, and replace it every 10 years.Open curtains and let the sun in during the dayKeep doors closed to trap heat in the room you're in. You can place curtains or blankets over your doors for extra insulation.Embrace the daylight. "If it's sunny outside, open the curtains so the sun heats the room, then shut them when the sun sets to keep the heat in," says Rebecca.Image source, Olga Pankova/Getty ImagesImage caption, Sunlight can help keep rooms comfortable for longer before you need to switch the heating on"If you're using a hot appliance, let the heat into the room," says Lianne Macfarlane, 40, from Cheshire. She recommends leaving your oven door open after using it to help warm your kitchen, though this isn't advised if you have small children who could injure themselves.As well as curtains, other soft furnishings like rugs can help keep a room warm, says Seymour.Image source, Elin DavisImage caption, Elin Davis fires up her log burner when it gets coldIf you have a fireplace, lighting a fire to warm the room you're in can be cheaper than turning on the central heating for your whole house. Elin Davis, 30, from South Wales, says her log burner is more economical than turning her heating on - though she added that "logs can cost quite a bit these days".Insulate your windows with bubble wrapGaps around doors can cause heat to escape, so place draught excluders around your door frames. You don't need to buy them - you can use towels or stuff socks into a pair of tights.When it's a windy day, Seymour recommends looking for other draughts in your house and either finding ways to seal these spots yourself or calling in a professional to help. These include using foam strips, sealant and specialist chimney draught excluders if you don't use your fireplace. Things such as extractor fans and purpose-built ventilation shouldn't be blocked, she adds.If your windows are single-glazed, then Sophie Burr of charity National Energy Action suggests looking at secondary glazing or investing in thermal curtains to help keep the heat in. Or for a cheaper option, some people suggest placing bubble wrap on your windows.Even though it may be tempting, don't keep your windows closed all the time. Seymour notes that it's important to allow some ventilation in your house to prevent damp.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, If you're after cheap insulation, especially if your window panes are single-glazed, then placing bubble wrap on them might helpUse central heating wisely"I wouldn't recommend not having your heating on at all," says Seymour, pointing to both the health issues this can cause as well as how pipes can freeze over.But there are ways you can use heating wisely. These include checking whether your energy supplier offers cheaper prices at off-peak times, bleeding your radiators so that they're more efficient, and turning your heating up in small increments until you reach the right temperature. If you have furniture in front of your radiator, then try moving it to avoid blocking the heat.You can also buy dedicated radiator foil or make your own with kitchen foil to reflect the heat back into the room rather than losing it through the walls, says Burr. She points out that about 35% of heat that comes from radiators is lost through walls.Cora Harrison, 34, from Wakefield, says that she only turns the radiators on in the rooms her family is using and keeps the heating on at a low level when they're on holiday to avoid mould or pipes bursting. Some radiators have a snowflake symbol on the valve that activates the frost protection setting, meaning that if the room gets very cold, the radiator warms slightly to stop the pipes from bursting.Another way to potentially reduce energy bills is to lower the flow temperature of your combi boiler. If you book a boiler service, an engineer can do this for you.You can also find free warm spaces such as libraries and community centres in your area by looking online or contacting the council. Some spaces also provide free hot drinks.Will energy bills rise further?Household energy prices are set to soar in January, with a typical bill expected to jump by £276 a year, according to a forecast last month from consultancy Cornwall Insight. The 16% predicted increase would mark the biggest rise for four years.Rising bills are "particularly concerning for people with kids, people with health conditions and the elderly," says Emily Jeremy, project manager at Manchester South Central Foodbank.An estimated 9.4% of households in England lived in fuel poverty in 2025, according to the latest government figures, external.Rodney Winchester, 65, from Thetford, who spoke to BBC News through the charity Christians Against Poverty, says he's "extremely worried" about rising energy prices. Because of health conditions, he says he has to keep the heating on throughout winter but is concerned he won't be able to afford it."It's so scary," Rodney says, adding that he's been cutting back on food spending and keeps getting ill in the cold weather.If you are struggling with prices, the debt charity StepChange recommends checking whether you qualify for any additional support, like the Warm Home Discount and Winter Fuel Payment. It also advises contacting your energy supplier, which may be able to agree an affordable repayment plan or discuss support schemes.Get in touchAre you affected by issues covered in this story?   Share your experiences.

schema.headline: How to heat your home without turning on the heating
